title: Incidence and Predictors of Meditation-Related Unusual Experiences and Adverse Effects in a Representative Sample of Meditators in the United States
venue: Clinical Psychological Science (published online 2025-01-06). Read: authors' manuscript of 14 MAY 2024 deposited at osf.io/24xe9; the published version was not reachable (subscription) and may differ.

selection.evidence: Opened 2026-10-23 because my own abstract-only record vandam2025-meditation-adverse-effects-representative (2026-10-17) carries the open question 'Retrieve OSF 3mn9y; ... is the retreat effect robust to the adjustment schlosser2019 needed (years, type)?', and OSF, down then, answered today. Prior expectation, stated before reading results: schlosser2019 and goldberg2022 found an early-onset, flat-in-years prevalence; I want to know whether this sample shows it.

cost.compute_notes: 2026-10-17: abstract only (OSF 503). 2026-10-23: deposit fetched (10 files, ~5 MB, each against OSF's sha256), manuscript read in full (27 pp.), authors' R read, everything recomputed in Python (no R on this host): .rds read with the `rdata` package through a custom data.frame constructor. Data not committed (participant IDs); reanalysis/fetch.py regenerates it. All scripts run in seconds.

claims.statement: In a population-based survey of 886 US adults stratified by lifetime meditation experience, 96.6% reported an unusual experience, 58.4% an adverse effect (IME), 78.3% one or more MRAES items, 31.4% a challenging/difficult/distressing experience, and 9.1% functional impairment from adverse effects.
claims.scope: Cross-sectional, US, Prolific, data collected Aug-Sep 2022; 886 retained of 1,102 who passed data checks (216 removed for low or excessive response variability or multivariate outlyingness); approximately representative on age, gender, race/ethnicity, not on education (60.6% bachelor's or higher).

quantities.name: meditation_unusual_experience_prevalence
quantities.source: manuscript p.13 and the count hard-coded in Predictors_and_Incidence_8Apr2024.R line 26

quantities.name: meditation_unusual_experience_prevalence_from_deposit
quantities.source: reanalysis/v01, v02: ue_tot > 0, rebuilt from the 30 item intensities (matches the deposited ue_tot in 886/886 rows)

quantities.name: meditation_adverse_effect_functional_impairment_prevalence
quantities.source: v01; reproduces exactly; asked only of the 278 who endorsed the generic item

quantities.name: ime_ae_prevalence_bounds_under_missing_valence
quantities.baseline: missing (never-asked) valence counted as not unpleasant / as unpleasant; imputed: 0.5835

our_assessment.why: Every adverse-effect count reproduces exactly from the deposit (517, 694, 278, 81, 34). The unusual-experience count does not. 856 is hard-coded in the authors' script, but the data give 861 (97.2%) by the stated definition, rebuilt item by item. And 856 is exactly the number of CURRENT meditators (MED.Screener = 1), a likely mix-up. More important for anyone quoting these rates: they belong to the instrument as administered. Two questionnaire features were randomised, and each moves a headline by more than 10 points. Fixed item order gives 63.4% IME adverse effects, randomised order 52.8%. Asking about unusual experiences before adverse effects gives 37.4% on the generic item, the reverse order 24.9%. The imputed valences, by contrast, barely matter: bounds 57.7-59.7%.

claims.statement: H1b supported: the rate of endorsing the single generic AE item (31.38%) is not significantly different from the 32.3% reported by Goldberg et al. (2022) (chi2(1) = 0.07, p = .795), with a 91.47% posterior probability of practical equivalence.

our_assessment.why: The pooled test reproduces. But the pooled 31.4% is the average of two randomised arms that differ by 12.5 points on this very item: 24.9% when the AE block came first, 37.4% when the unusual-experience block came first (p = 6e-5). Against Goldberg's 32.3%, the first arm is significantly LOWER (p = .021) and the second is higher, not significantly. 'Consistent with prior work' is therefore a property of the 52/48 mix of the two arms, not of US meditators. Which arm is comparable to Goldberg depends on what preceded the item in that survey, and the manuscript does not say.

claims.statement: An adverse effect per the IME is endorsement of any of the 30 IME items at slight or greater intensity and 'modestly unpleasant or greater' valence (Measures, p.10); Results report the rate at 'mildly unpleasant or worse' (p.13).

quantities.name: ime_ae_prevalence_mildly_unpleasant_threshold
quantities.source: v02 (valence code <= 3; reproduces the deposited iue.number in 886/886 rows)

our_assessment.why: The headline is computed at code <= 3 ('mildly unpleasant'). That is the deviation the Method section lists as (b). But the Measures paragraph still defines the outcome as 'modestly unpleasant or greater', which gives 42.2%, 16 points lower. The data dictionary calls it '>= slightly unpleasant', a label the 7-point scale does not have. A reader taking the Measures sentence at its word would misread the number.

claims.statement: Meditation experience was not robustly associated with adverse effects; retreat attendance was associated with the generic AE definition and with functional impairment; psychological distress was associated with all AE definitions.
claims.scope: Robust multiple regression (robustbase lmrob/glmrob), Table 3; zero-order associations, Table 4.

quantities.name: retreat_or_impairment_adjusted
quantities.baseline: adjusted for log10 hours, years, K10, psychoticism; raw OR 1.78 (p .036)

our_assessment.why: Reproduced in substance with ordinary (not robust) models: the retreat association survives adjustment for dose and distress, generic AE OR 1.48 and impairment OR 2.13 (p = .01). This answers the 2026-10-17 open question: robust to the adjustment schlosser2019 needed. The 'experience' finding needs a sharper wording. The zero-order association of the IME rate with hours is NEGATIVE (p = .005), and the rate falls from 68.5% (<= 1 year) to 42.4% (> 20 years). It disappears once distress is held fixed (c6). Table 3 contains one impossible entry (c5).

claims.statement: Table 3: lifetime experience (hours) predicts the number of unusual experiences, beta = 0.171** (SE 0.171).

our_assessment.why: Arithmetic on the printed numbers. A beta equal to its own SE cannot be significant at .01. One of the two numbers is a transcription error. The logistic columns of the same table are consistent once SEs are read as delta-method SEs of the odds ratio, which suggests the typo is in this cell alone. Not re-estimated: robustbase's MM-estimator is not available here, and statsmodels' RLM is a different estimator.

claims.statement: Lifetime adverse-effect incidence falls with practice in this sample (IME: 68.5% at <= 1 year to 42.4% at > 20 years), and the fall is carried by distress: less-experienced meditators are more distressed (Spearman K10 vs log hours -0.215), and with K10 and psychoticism held fixed the hours and years gradients vanish among current meditators (IME hours +0.09, p .55; years -0.018, p .13); for the generic item the adjusted hours gradient turns positive (+0.55 per log10 hour, p .0008).
claims.scope: 856 current meditators (meditated in the past 12 months); only 30 lapsed respondents, 1 of whom stopped because of a bad experience, so attrition cannot be measured inside this sample.

quantities.name: generic_ae_adjusted_slope_per_log10_hour_current
quantities.baseline: adjusted for years, K10, psychoticism; p = 0.00083

our_assessment.why: A LIFETIME incidence cannot fall with exposure within one population. Across people, it falls if the harmed practise less afterwards, if old events are forgotten, or if who starts meditating has changed. The data cannot tell these apart. The sample recruited people with meditation experience and holds only 30 lapsed respondents. Adjusting for distress removes the gradient. But K10 covers the past 30 days, and it may itself be a consequence of adverse effects, so the adjustment is conditioning on a possible mediator. Attrition of the harmed is argued AGAINST by the lapsed respondents who exist. Here they report the generic item less often (23% of 30, vs 32% of current meditators). In goldberg2022 lapsed practitioners also report fewer adverse effects. What remains is composition: the less experienced are more distressed. That holds whether distressed people start meditating more recently, accumulate fewer hours, or stop. The safe reading: in cross-sectional practitioner surveys, 'experienced meditators report fewer adverse effects' is not evidence that practice protects, and once distress is held fixed it is not even an association. Consistent with schlosser2019's flat lifetime prevalence across years.

claims.statement: Valence was asked for at most 50 randomly chosen items per person, and missing valences were filled by random-forest multiple imputation. The imputation changed no observed value, and the IME adverse-effect rate is bounded between 57.7% and 59.7% whatever the missing valences were; 6 of the 517 cases rest only on imputed values.
claims.scope: All 103 valence items; 27,548 observed and 63,710 never-asked cells.

our_assessment.why: A check that came back clean, recorded because it is evidence. On the first run it looked like a defect, with the imputation apparently overwriting 69% of observed values. The cause was my reader: the Python `rdata` package returns R's NA_integer_ as -2147483648, so every missing cell compared as 'unpleasant'. Fixed in reanalysis/load_rds.py, and the trap is recorded there.

relations.why: Retreat participation positively associated with adverse effects in both; here it survives adjustment for hours, years and distress (impairment OR 2.13).
Single-item practitioner prevalence (25.4%) sits next to this sample's single-item 24.9-37.4% (by framing arm), not its instrument-based 58-97%.
H1b-d compare against Goldberg's 140/434 and 217/434, using an adapted 14-item MRAES with a different response format.
A headline rate that belongs to how the question was put: elicitation format there, item order and block order here, each worth more than 10 points.

open_questions: Read the published (2025) version: does it report the order and framing effects, correct 856, and fix the Measures threshold sentence?
Which framing arm is comparable to Goldberg et al. 2022, i.e. what preceded the generic item in that survey?

Attrition cannot be measured here (30 lapsed respondents). A sample that includes people who stopped meditating is the only way to tell survivorship from protection; vieten2018 or a panel with lapsed practitioners.

PARTLY ANSWERED 2026-10-23 (vandam2024-ime-psychometrics c3, c4): the Mahalanobis p < .001 rule flags 12.5% of a no-outlier copula of these items and selects high endorsers (rho .84), so the 159-case exclusion very likely removed high-endorsement profiles; plausible effect on the IME adverse-effect rate ~ +4 points (58.4% -> ~62%). Which variables entered the distance is still unknown, and the rows are not in the deposit.
